content: Women should be educated about the initiation of breastfeeding, supplementation protocols, and the practice of rooming-in. They must also be informed about potential challenges, such as breast engorgement or concerns about insufficient milk production, and provided with strategies to address these issues effectively. Antenatal breastfeeding counseling should be personalized to meet the specific needs of the woman and her family, addressing their concerns and questions. This counseling must be delivered sensitively, taking into account the social and cultural context of each family. Breastfeeding discussions should ideally begin during the first or second antenatal visit to allow sufficient time to address any challenges. This is particularly important in settings where women have limited antenatal visits or initiate care late in pregnancy. Women who deliver prematurely may not have adequate opportunities to discuss breastfeeding if these conversations are delayed until late in pregnancy. Information on breastfeeding should be provided in multiple formats, including printed or online materials in languages that mothers, including those who are illiterate, can understand. However, it is important to note that not all women will read this information, and it may not address their specific questions. The information provided must be free from conflicts of interest, as stipulated in the guidance on ending inappropriate promotion of infant and young child foods. Special populations, such as pregnant adolescents, women with high-risk pregnancies, or those expecting infants with known congenital anomalies, should begin discussions with knowledgeable providers as early as possible to address the unique circumstances of feeding a premature, low-birth-weight, or sick baby. Global standards for antenatal breastfeeding discussions include emphasizing the importance of breastfeeding, global recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, the risks of formula or other breast-milk substitutes, and the continued importance of breastfeeding after six months when complementary foods are introduced. Other key topics include the significance of immediate and sustained skin-to-skin contact, early initiation of breastfeeding, rooming-in, proper positioning and attachment, and recognizing feeding cues. At least 80% of mothers who receive prenatal care at a facility should report having received counseling on breastfeeding. Additionally, at least 80% of these mothers should be able to adequately describe two of the discussed topics. Immediate postnatal care should facilitate uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and support mothers in initiating breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth. Immediate skin-to-skin contact promotes the newborn's natural rooting reflex, which helps establish the behavior of seeking and suckling at the breast. It also populates the newborn's microbiome, prevents hypothermia, and triggers breast milk production, accelerating lactogenesis. Early initiation of breastfeeding has been shown to reduce infant mortality risk. Skin-to-skin contact should begin immediately after birth, regardless of the delivery method, and should last uninterrupted for at least 60 minutes. This practice is feasible even after cesarean sections performed under local anesthesia. If general anesthesia is used, skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding initiation can begin once the mother is alert enough to hold the infant. Medically unstable mothers or infants may need to delay breastfeeding initiation, but they should still be supported to provide skin-to-skin contact and breastfeed as soon as they are able. Skin-to-skin contact is particularly important for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Kangaroo mother care, involving early, continuous, and prolonged skin-to-skin contact, should be the primary mode of care for stable preterm infants due to its demonstrated benefits in survival, thermal protection, and breastfeeding initiation. Preterm infants as early as 27 weeks' gestation may be able to root, attach to the breast, and suckle if they are stable and free from severe apnea, desaturation, or bradycardia. However, effective breastfeeding initiation may be challenging if the sucking reflex is not yet established or the mother has not begun sufficient milk secretion. Early and frequent milk expression is critical for stimulating milk production and secretion in preterm infants who cannot yet suckle. The goal should be to transition to direct and exclusive breastfeeding whenever possible, facilitated by prolonged skin-to-skin contact. At least 80% of mothers of term infants should report that their babies were placed in skin-to-skin contact with them immediately or within five minutes after birth, lasting for at least one hour unless medically justified. Similarly, at least 80% of mothers should report that their babies were put to the breast within one hour after birth unless there were documented medical reasons for delay. Breastfeeding support is essential for mothers to initiate and maintain breastfeeding and manage common difficulties. While breastfeeding is a natural behavior, most mothers require practical assistance to learn how to breastfeed effectively. Even experienced mothers may face new challenges with a newborn. Postnatal breastfeeding counseling and support have been shown to increase breastfeeding rates up to six months of age. Early adjustments to positioning and attachment can prevent later breastfeeding problems, and frequent coaching helps build maternal confidence. Mothers should receive individualized attention, with first-time mothers and those who have not breastfed before requiring extra support. Even mothers with previous children may need assistance if they had negative breastfeeding experiences. Practical support for preterm infants, including late preterm newborns, is particularly critical to establish and maintain breast milk production. Many mothers of preterm infants face their own health challenges and require motivation and additional support for milk expression. Late preterm infants are generally able to breastfeed exclusively but are at higher risk for jaundice, hypoglycemia, and feeding difficulties, necessitating increased vigilance. Mothers of twins also need extra support, especially for positioning and attachment. Teaching mothers to breastfeed should include demonstrating proper positioning and attachment, which are crucial for stimulating milk production and ensuring adequate milk intake. Direct observation of a feeding session is necessary to confirm that the infant can attach to and suckle at the breast and that milk transfer is occurring. Facility staff should educate mothers on managing engorged breasts, ensuring a good milk supply, preventing cracked and sore nipples, and evaluating milk intake. Mothers should also be taught how to express breast milk to maintain lactation if temporarily separated from their infants. There is no definitive evidence that one method of milk expression (hand expression, manual pump, or electric pump) is superior, so any method may be taught based on the mother's context. Hand expression has the advantage of being available anywhere and allowing the mother to relieve pressure or express milk without a pump. However, pumps may carry a higher risk of microbial contamination if not easily cleaned. Mothers should also be supported in the collection and storage of expressed milk. Breastfed newborns should not be given any food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated. Introducing other foods or fluids in the first few days after birth interferes with the establishment of breast milk production. Newborns' stomachs are small and easily filled, and feeding them other substances reduces their vigorous suckling at the breast, leading to insufficient milk production and a cycle of supplementation that can result in breastfeeding failure. Supplementation with artificial milk alters the intestinal microflora and increases the risk of disease. Mothers should be discouraged from giving any food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically necessary. Very few conditions preclude breastfeeding or necessitate the use of breast-milk substitutes. Infants should be assessed for signs of inadequate milk intake and supplemented only when indicated. Routine supplementation is rarely necessary in the first few days of life.
